```{r setup}
library(dplyr)
library(metafor)
library(netmeta)

source("R/hta_methods.R")

fmt_ci <- function(est, lo, hi, d = 2) {
  f <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)
  paste0(f(est), " (", f(lo), ", ", f(hi), ")")
}
fmt_p <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p))

labels <- c(A = "No contact", B = "Self-help", C = "Individual counselling",
            D = "Group counselling")

data(smokingcessation, package = "netmeta")
smk <- smokingcessation %>% mutate(study = row_number())
```

## The data

The network holds 24 studies of four ways to help people stop smoking. The
outcome is whether a person had quit at follow-up. Most studies compare an
active intervention with no contact. Two studies have three arms.

Source: Hasselblad V. Meta-analysis of multitreatment studies.
*Medical Decision Making* 1998, 18(1), 37-43. They are also a common
teaching example for network meta-analysis. They ship with the R
package `{netmeta}`.

```{r designs}
smk %>%
  mutate(Design = ifelse(treat3 == "", paste(treat1, treat2, sep = " vs "),
                         paste(treat1, treat2, treat3, sep = " vs "))) %>%
  count(Design, name = "Studies")
```

`r paste0(names(labels), " = ", labels, collapse = ", ")`.

## 1. Anchored indirect comparison by the Bucher method

The question: how does **self-help** compare with **individual counselling**?
Only two studies compare them directly, and one of those has three arms. Many
more studies compare each of them with **no contact**, the common
comparator. The Bucher method asks what those studies say about self-help
against counselling. Bucher and colleagues (1997) showed how to
combine the two comparisons without breaking randomisation. On the log odds
ratio scale:

- log OR(self-help vs counselling) = log OR(self-help vs no contact) - log OR(counselling vs no contact)
- Var = Var(self-help vs no contact) + Var(counselling vs no contact)

Each ingredient is a pooled estimate from its own set of trials. To keep the
two ingredients independent, only two-arm studies are used here. A three-arm
study would put correlated contrasts on both sides of the subtraction.

### Step 1. Each study's log odds ratio by hand

```{r study-effects}
# Log odds ratio of quitting, active (treat2) vs no contact (treat1).
# log_or_hand() adds 0.5 to every cell of a study with a zero cell.
study_lor <- function(d) {
  cbind(study = d$study, log_or_hand(d$event2, d$n2, d$event1, d$n1))
}

two_arm <- smk %>% filter(treat3 == "")
sh <- study_lor(two_arm %>% filter(treat1 == "A", treat2 == "B"))  # self-help vs no contact
ic <- study_lor(two_arm %>% filter(treat1 == "A", treat2 == "C"))  # counselling vs no contact

bind_rows(
  sh %>% mutate(Comparison = "Self-help vs no contact"),
  ic %>% mutate(Comparison = "Individual counselling vs no contact")
) %>%
  transmute(Comparison, Study = study,
            `OR (95% CI)` = fmt_ci(exp(yi), exp(yi - 1.96 * sqrt(vi)), exp(yi + 1.96 * sqrt(vi))),
            `Zero cell corrected` = ifelse(corrected, "yes", ""))
```

### Step 2. Pool each comparison, then subtract

```{r bucher}
fe_sh <- fe_hand(sh$yi, sh$vi)
fe_ic <- fe_hand(ic$yi, ic$vi)
bu    <- bucher_hand(fe_sh$est, fe_sh$se, fe_ic$est, fe_ic$se)

data.frame(
  Comparison = c("Self-help vs no contact (direct, pooled)",
                 "Individual counselling vs no contact (direct, pooled)",
                 "Self-help vs individual counselling (indirect, Bucher)"),
  Studies = c(nrow(sh), nrow(ic), ""),
  `log OR` = round(c(fe_sh$est, fe_ic$est, bu$est), 4),
  SE = round(c(fe_sh$se, fe_ic$se, bu$se), 4),
  `OR (95% CI)` = c(fmt_ci(exp(fe_sh$est), exp(fe_sh$lower), exp(fe_sh$upper)),
                    fmt_ci(exp(fe_ic$est), exp(fe_ic$lower), exp(fe_ic$upper)),
                    fmt_ci(exp(bu$est), exp(bu$lower), exp(bu$upper))),
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

### Step 3. Confirm with `netmeta`

Fed only these two-arm studies, `netmeta` sees a star-shaped network with no
contact in the middle. Its common-effect estimate for self-help against
individual counselling is then exactly the Bucher estimate.

```{r bucher-netmeta}
pw_all <- pairwise(treat = list(treat1, treat2, treat3),
                   event = list(event1, event2, event3),
                   n = list(n1, n2, n3), data = smk, studlab = study, sm = "OR")
pw_star <- subset(pw_all, studlab %in% c(sh$study, ic$study))
nm_star <- netmeta(pw_star, common = TRUE, random = FALSE, reference.group = "A")

data.frame(
  Source = c("Hand (Bucher)", "netmeta, star network"),
  `log OR` = c(bu$est, nm_star$TE.common["B", "C"]),
  SE = c(bu$se, nm_star$seTE.common["B", "C"]),
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

The indirect odds ratio is `r fmt_ci(exp(bu$est), exp(bu$lower), exp(bu$upper))`.
Self-help appears to help fewer people quit than individual counselling.

The two pooled inputs above use the fixed-effect model. The
counselling-versus-no-contact studies are very heterogeneous, so a
random-effects version is the more honest sensitivity analysis:

```{r bucher-re}
re_sh <- rma(sh$yi, sh$vi, method = "REML")
re_ic <- rma(ic$yi, ic$vi, method = "REML")
bu_re <- bucher_hand(re_sh$beta[1], re_sh$se, re_ic$beta[1], re_ic$se)
data.frame(
  Model = c("Fixed effect", "Random effects (REML)"),
  `I^2, counselling vs no contact` = sprintf("%.0f%%", c(rma(ic$yi, ic$vi, method = "FE")$I2, re_ic$I2)),
  `Indirect OR (95% CI)` = c(fmt_ci(exp(bu$est), exp(bu$lower), exp(bu$upper)),
                             fmt_ci(exp(bu_re$est), exp(bu_re$lower), exp(bu_re$upper))),
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

With random effects the interval
`r fmt_ci(exp(bu_re$est), exp(bu_re$lower), exp(bu_re$upper))` is much wider.
The fixed-effect result overstates the certainty.

## 2. The assumptions in plain words

**Similarity.** The self-help trials and the counselling trials must be alike
in everything that changes how well an intervention works. That covers
patients, settings, how "no contact" was delivered, the definition of
quitting and the length of follow-up. If they differ, the subtraction
compares more than the two interventions.

**Effect modifiers.** These are the characteristics that change the relative
effect, for example how motivated people are to quit. A difference in a
purely prognostic factor, one that changes the quit rate but not the odds
ratio, does not bias an anchored comparison. A difference in an effect
modifier does, and randomisation inside each trial cannot remove it. The bias can only be judged from
what the trials report.

**Why the interval is wider than in either trial.** The indirect estimate is
a difference of two independent estimates. Each carries its own sampling
error, and variances of independent estimates add. Here the standard error
is `r sprintf("%.3f", bu$se)`, against `r sprintf("%.3f", fe_sh$se)` and
`r sprintf("%.3f", fe_ic$se)` for the two inputs. An indirect comparison is
always less precise than a direct trial of the same size. When the two inputs are equally precise, the indirect estimate has the
precision of a direct trial with a quarter of their combined patients.

## 3. A network meta-analysis

A network meta-analysis uses all studies at once, including the three-arm
ones and any direct comparisons between active interventions. Every
comparison then draws on direct and indirect evidence together. The
frequentist method in `netmeta` is weighted least squares on the network.
Three-arm studies are handled so that their correlated contrasts are not
counted twice.

```{r nma}
nma <- netmeta(pw_all, common = TRUE, random = TRUE, reference.group = "A",
               method.tau = "REML", small.values = "undesirable")
```

### Network graph

```{r netgraph, fig.height = 5}
# No contact (A) in the centre: every pair is connected, and this layout
# draws the network without crossing lines. Order of nma$trts: A, B, C, D.
netgraph(nma, labels = nma$trts, plastic = FALSE,
         thickness = "number.of.studies", number.of.studies = TRUE,
         multiarm = FALSE, points = TRUE, cex.points = 3, col.points = "#0072B2",
         col = "grey40", cex = 1.4, offset = 0.05,
         xpos = c(0, -1.4, 1.4, 0), ypos = c(-0.1, -0.9, -0.9, 1.5),
         adj = rbind(c(-0.9, -0.6), c(0.5, 1), c(0.5, 1), c(0.5, 0)))
title(sub = paste(paste(names(labels), labels, sep = " = "), collapse = ",  "))
```

Each line is a direct comparison. Its width and number show how many
studies made it, counting each three-arm study once for each of its pairs.
Every pair of interventions has at least one direct study. So every
comparison combines direct and indirect evidence.

### League table

Each cell gives the random-effects network odds ratio of quitting for the
row intervention against the column intervention, with its 95% confidence
interval. Values above 1 favour the row.

```{r league}
# Cell [row, column]: network OR of the row intervention vs the column one.
ord <- c("A", "B", "C", "D")
lt <- outer(ord, ord, Vectorize(function(r, c) {
  if (r == c) return(labels[[r]])
  fmt_ci(exp(nma$TE.random[r, c]), exp(nma$lower.random[r, c]), exp(nma$upper.random[r, c]))
}))
dimnames(lt) <- list(labels[ord], labels[ord])
as.data.frame(lt, check.names = FALSE)
```

`netmeta::netleague()` gives the same numbers in a compact form. Its lower
triangle holds the network estimates (column against row) and its upper
triangle the direct estimates (row against column).

```{r nma-summary}
data.frame(
  Comparison = paste(labels[c("B", "C", "D")], "vs no contact"),
  `OR (95% CI), random effects` = fmt_ci(exp(nma$TE.random[c("B", "C", "D"), "A"]),
                                         exp(nma$lower.random[c("B", "C", "D"), "A"]),
                                         exp(nma$upper.random[c("B", "C", "D"), "A"])),
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

Heterogeneity is large: τ² = `r sprintf("%.2f", nma$tau^2)` and I² =
`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * nma$I2)`%. Every active intervention looks better than
no contact on average. The intervals are wide, and the one for self-help
includes 1.

### Direct against indirect evidence

Consistency means that direct and indirect evidence on the same comparison
agree. Node splitting separates them for each comparison and tests the
difference. A closed loop is needed for a comparison to have both.

```{r netsplit}
ns <- netsplit(nma)
data.frame(
  Comparison = ns$comparison,
  `Direct studies` = ns$k,
  `Direct OR` = sprintf("%.2f", exp(ns$direct.random$TE)),
  `Indirect OR` = sprintf("%.2f", exp(ns$indirect.random$TE)),
  `Network OR` = sprintf("%.2f", exp(ns$random$TE)),
  `p for difference` = fmt_p(ns$compare.random$p),
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r decomp}
dd <- decomp.design(nma)
q_between <- dd$Q.decomp["Between designs", ]   # common-effect model
q_random  <- dd$Q.inc.random                    # allowing for heterogeneity
```

No comparison shows a clear disagreement between direct and indirect
evidence in the random-effects model. Self-help against individual
counselling is a useful example. The two direct studies give OR
`r sprintf("%.2f", exp(ns$direct.random$TE[ns$comparison == "B:C"]))`, the
indirect evidence `r sprintf("%.2f", exp(ns$indirect.random$TE[ns$comparison == "B:C"]))`.
They point in different directions, yet the test cannot tell them apart
(p = `r fmt_p(ns$compare.random$p[ns$comparison == "B:C"])`) because the
direct evidence is so thin. The design-by-treatment test of
inconsistency for the whole network gives Q = `r sprintf("%.1f", q_between$Q)`
on `r q_between$df` degrees of freedom (p = `r fmt_p(q_between$pval)`), under the
common-effect model. Once between-study heterogeneity is allowed for, it
falls to Q = `r sprintf("%.1f", q_random$Q)` (p = `r fmt_p(q_random$pval)`). These tests have little power. Failing to
reject consistency does not prove it, and it says nothing about
transitivity, which is a judgement about the trials and not a statistical
test.

Population-adjusted methods, for when this anchored approach is not possible
or not enough, are described on the [next page](03b-population-adjusted.qmd).
